addressed_problems.content: The SoftNet method protects base-session knowledge by freezing the major subnetwork (weights with top-c% magnitude, m=1) after base training. However, if any subsequent tuning inadvertently adjusts those major weights, the previously acquired knowledge can be lost. The paper explicitly leaves unresolved how to design an online mechanism that detects when the major subnetwork is at risk of being overwritten and adapts the model sparsity or protection level so that new-session learners can reliably preserve base knowledge without requiring revisiting past data.

SoftNet explicitly separates parameters into major and minor subnetworks based on magnitude and exposes the resulting mask structure. This clear delineation makes the selected essential parameters vulnerable to intentional model attacks or information leakage about the task knowledge stored in the mask. The paper identifies as an open engineering challenge the development of compact or compressed encodings (e.g., binary mask compression) that reduce model capacity while also protecting the privacy of the task-specific knowledge encoded in the soft or binary masks.

The current SoftNet procedure freezes the major subnetwork and adapts only a small set of minor parameters (m_minor) during a modest number of few-shot incremental sessions. For full class-incremental learning (CIL) regimes with much longer sequences of incoming classes, the fixed capacity of the minor subnetwork may become insufficient and the frozen major subnetwork cannot accommodate new knowledge. The paper explicitly leaves for future work the investigation of dynamic capacity expansion or reallocation strategies (e.g., expanding parameters or reallocating minor capacity) that would allow SoftNet to scale to long sequences without revisiting prior data.

SoftNet's performance depends critically on the chosen capacity c (the percentage of weights in the major subnetwork) and on the architecture (e.g., ResNet18 vs. ResNet20 show different optimal sparsity levels). The paper provides empirical curves but no principled rule for selecting c or automatically adapting the softness per layer or per dataset for arbitrary architectures. Determining such guidelines or an adaptive mechanism to choose the mask sparsity and softness based on data properties or architecture remains an open problem.

Few-shot class-incremental learning (FSCIL) requires a model to learn a sequence of class-incremental sessions where the base session has many labeled examples but each later session provides only a few examples per new class. Under this setting two intertwined scientific problems arise that the prior literature did not satisfactorily resolve. First, catastrophic forgetting: updating all model parameters to accommodate new classes causes destructive interference with parameters that encode previously learned classes, producing large performance drops on earlier classes; existing remedies (constraint-based regularizers, rehearsal/memory, architecture expansion or hard-masking/pruning) either rely on revisiting data, add architectural overhead, or use hard (binary) isolation that is not flexible enough for FSCIL. Second, overfitting to scarce new-class samples: with only K-shot data per new class, naïve fine-tuning of large networks or even of subnetworks tends to overfit, producing poor generalization on the new classes and exacerbating forgetting. As a result, before this work there was no simple, computationally efficient procedure that (a) identifies within a dense network a parameter subspace that reliably retains base-session knowledge, (b) simultaneously leaves flexible, regularized capacity for rapid, low-overfit adaptation to later few-shot sessions, and (c) provides operational rules (which parameters/layers to update, how to perform inference) with quantitative evidence on standard FSCIL benchmarks. This gap prevented practitioners from obtaining both strong base-class retention and robust few-shot adaptation in a light-weight, single-backbone setup without expensive retraining or structural expansion.

nodes.content: In FSCIL, prior formulations of the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis focused on binary "winning tickets" (hard masks) that either select or remove parameters. Such hard masks cannot simultaneously serve as a robust reservoir of base-class knowledge (which should resist change) and a flexible adaptation substrate for new few-shot classes (which requires tunable parameters). Without the RLTH framing there was no simple hypothesis guiding the design of masks that are both protective and adaptive: practitioners lacked the conceptual basis to seek smooth, partially-weighted subnetworks that act as implicit regularizers, so methods either used expensive retraining/pruning cycles or architectures that expanded capacity. RLTH targets that gap by proposing that smooth subnetworks exist and are useful for FSCIL.

FSCIL requires a practical procedure that (i) identifies which parameters must be protected to avoid forgetting and which may be safely adapted to learn new K-shot classes, (ii) can be trained efficiently in the base session without repeated prune-retrain cycles, and (iii) provides a smooth regularization mechanism to prevent overfitting during few-shot updates. Prior architecture-based approaches either expanded the model, required iterative pruning and retraining (computationally expensive), or used binary masks that were too rigid for a trade-off between stability and plasticity. There was no single, efficient algorithm that jointly learns a parameterized mask and model weights, produces a mixed binary/continuous mask supporting selective freezing, and prescribes a light-weight incremental update rule; SoftNet fills this operational gap by providing a single-backbone, jointly-trained soft-mask procedure enabling selective, regularized updates during FSCIL.

During few-shot incremental updates, Euclidean-based or softmax cross-entropy fine-tuning of a small number of weights can produce biased or unstable similarity measurements between embeddings, causing poor new-class discrimination and aggravating forgetting. Prior FSCIL fine-tuning approaches either used Euclidean prototype metrics or full-network updates that were not robust in scarce-data regimes. A normalized, direction-based similarity (cosine distance) during minor-subnetwork fine-tuning stabilizes prototype estimation from few examples and provides a consistent similarity metric for NCM inference; describing this explicit fine-tuning+NCM pipeline addresses the practical need for a robust, light-weight inference rule compatible with SoftNet's selective updates.

Before this work, existing FSCIL methods either suffered larger drops in accuracy over incremental sessions, required heavier rehearsal/architecture changes, or were computationally expensive; practitioners lacked quantitative evidence that a single-backbone, masking-based approach can simultaneously retain base-class performance while enabling K-shot learning of many subsequent sessions. Concrete numerical benchmarks across sessions are required to demonstrate practical viability. By reporting session-by-session accuracies and the final-session values on CIFAR-100 and miniImageNet, SoftNet fills that empirical evidence gap and provides quantified improvements over prior baselines.

Practitioners need guidance about how many parameters to reserve as the major subnetwork vs. leave for minor (adaptive) weights: too small $c$ gives insufficient capacity to retain base knowledge, too large $c$ may leave insufficient flexible/regularized capacity for new classes or may over-regularize. Prior work did not provide systematic capacity-vs-performance curves for soft or hard subnetworks in FSCIL, leaving deployment choices ad-hoc. By empirically mapping accuracy as a function of $c$ and dataset, this conclusion supplies concrete evidence to guide practical $c$ selection and highlights dataset dependence.

FSCIL practitioners must know which layers to allow adaptation in order to maximize forward transfer while minimizing forgetting; without empirical layer-wise guidance, one might either update too many layers (causing forgetting/overfitting) or too few (losing adaptability). Prior literature lacked systematic layer-wise/architecture-wise ablations focused on selective minor-weight updates within a soft-mask framework. These ablations provide actionable rules (which conv block to fine-tune and how sparsity interacts with architecture) to apply SoftNet effectively.

One missing explanation for why pruning/masking can alleviate forgetting and overfitting was the optimization geometry: without evidence about the flatness of minima or embedding smoothness, it was unclear whether subnetworks merely reduce capacity or also alter the loss geometry in a way that supports robustness to incremental updates. Prior work touched on flat minima ideas but did not connect soft masks, empirical loss landscapes, and embedding separability in FSCIL. By showing flatter loss contours and improved t-SNE clustering for SoftNet, this conclusion helps explain the empirical stability of selective minor-weight updates.

Empirical gains from subnetworks suggest improved optimization behavior, but before this work there was little explicit connection between subnetwork selection and formal optimization quantities (Lipschitz constants, gradient ratios, convergence rates) tailored to soft masks. Practitioners and theorists lacked inequality-level statements comparing hard and soft masks' influence on gradient variation and on worst-case rates. By adapting Lipschitz-gradient reasoning and invoking existing subnetwork convergence bounds, the paper supplies a quantitative explanation for why softer (larger $\|\boldsymbol{m}\|_1$) subnetworks can produce flatter effective optimization dynamics and potentially faster convergence.

Regularized Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (RLTH): a randomly-initialized dense neural network contains a regularized (smooth/non-binary) subnetwork that can both retain prior class knowledge and provide room to learn new class knowledge through isolated training of the subnetwork; RLTH generalizes the binary-winning-ticket view by allowing continuous (soft) mask values in $[0,1]$ so that the subnetwork can act as a regularized parameter subspace for incremental few-shot adaptation.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 1 presents the Regularized Lottery Ticket Hypothesis as a claim of the paper. P11 identifies the absence of direct empirical validation: the paper does not verify that such a regularized subnetwork exists in a randomly initialized network independent of the SoftNet training procedure. No highlight supports this conclusion. The hypothesis is stated as inspiration rather than a validated result, but the conclusion XML presents it as a finding. The credibility of RLTH as an empirically supported scientific claim is low; the paper would need a separate verification experiment to establish it.

nodes.title: Regularized Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (RLTH)

nodes.content: Soft-SubNetworks (SoftNet) is a masking-based method for few-shot class incremental learning (FSCIL) that: (a) during the base session jointly optimizes model weights $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ and layer-wise weight scores $\boldsymbol{s}$ to produce a soft mask $\boldsymbol{m}_{soft}\in[0,1]^{|\boldsymbol{\theta}|}$ defined as $\boldsymbol{m}_{soft}=\boldsymbol{m}_{major}\oplus\boldsymbol{m}_{minor}$ where $\boldsymbol{m}_{major}=\mathbb{1}_{\text{top-}c\%}(\boldsymbol{s})$ is a binary mask selecting the top-$c\%$ scores and $\boldsymbol{m}_{minor}\sim U(0,1)$ is a continuous-valued mask on the remaining parameters; (b) updates $\boldsymbol{\theta}\leftarrow\boldsymbol{\theta}-\alpha\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\theta}}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{soft}\right)$ and updates scores $\boldsymbol{s}$ with a straight-through estimator $\boldsymbol{s}\leftarrow\boldsymbol{s}-\alpha\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\boldsymbol{s}}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{soft}\right)$ while training the base session; and (c) for incremental sessions freezes the major subnetwork ($\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{major}$) to preserve base knowledge and fine-tunes only the minor parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{minor}$ to learn novel classes.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 2 describes the SoftNet algorithm and its training/incremental update procedure. No weak points were identified that challenge the correctness of the description; the procedure is clearly specified in Algorithm 1 and Section 3.3. The conclusion is a factual operational description whose credibility derives directly from the paper text. Its effectiveness is evaluated separately in Conclusion 4. The prior is high.

nodes.title: Soft-SubNetworks (SoftNet) algorithm for few-shot class incremental learning

nodes.content: For incremental sessions, Soft-SubNetworks (SoftNet) fine-tunes the minor subnetwork using a metric-based classification loss with cosine distance: the per-sample loss is $\mathcal{L}_{m}(z;\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{soft})=-\sum_{o\in\mathcal{O}}\mathbb{1}(y=o)\log\frac{e^{-d(\boldsymbol{p}_o,f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{soft}))}}{\sum_{o_k\in\mathcal{O}}e^{-d(\boldsymbol{p}_{o_k},f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{soft}))}}$ where $d(\cdot,\cdot)$ is cosine distance and class prototypes $\boldsymbol{p}_o$ are computed as the mean embedding per class; at inference SoftNet uses nearest-class-mean (NCM) classification in feature space (Euclidean distance to stored prototypes) over all encountered classes $\mathcal{O}$.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 3 describes the metric-based fine-tuning loss (cosine distance) and NCM inference procedure. No weak points were identified; the procedure is explicitly defined in Section 4.1 (Eq. 5) and Section 4.2. The conclusion is a procedural specification. Its effectiveness is part of the overall empirical validation in Conclusion 4. The prior is high.

nodes.title: Metric-based fine-tuning and prototype/NCM inference for SoftNet

nodes.content: On standard few-shot class incremental learning (FSCIL) benchmarks with 60 base classes and 40 novel classes in 5-way 5-shot incremental sessions, Soft-SubNetworks (SoftNet) attains higher incremental accuracy than strong baselines. Examples of reported results (ResNet18 backbone): on CIFAR-100 SoftNet with $c=99\%$ achieves session-1 accuracy $72.62\%$ and session-9 accuracy $46.63\%$, producing a gap of $+1.35$ percentage points relative to the cRT baseline (classifier re-training, Kang et al., 2019); on miniImageNet SoftNet with $c=80\%$ achieves session-1 accuracy $76.63\%$ and session-9 accuracy $50.48\%$, a gap of $+5.63$ points relative to the cRT baseline. SoftNet also achieves superior or competitive accuracy on TOPIC splits of CIFAR-100 and miniImageNet and on the CUB-200-2011 dataset.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 4 claims state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks. Three premises (P1, P2, P3) weaken this claim. P1 is the most damaging: the paper's own Table 6 shows that on the miniImageNet TOPIC split, ALICE outperforms SoftNet, directly refuting the unqualified SOTA claim. P2 notes the absence of standard deviations, leaving statistical significance unquantified. P3 highlights that the best capacity c is selected per dataset, inflating apparent performance. No highlight offsets these risks (H2 and H3 support different conclusions). The credibility of the SOTA claim is moderate-low: SoftNet is competitive and often best on many settings, but the unqualified "state-of-the-art" assertion is not supported across all benchmarks, and the lack of error bars weakens the strength.

nodes.title: SoftNet yields state-of-the-art FSCIL accuracy on standard benchmarks

nodes.content: Soft-SubNetworks (SoftNet) overall accuracy monotonically improves with the selected major-subnetwork proportion $c$: increasing the proportion of parameters allocated to the major subnetwork (the top-$c\%$ selection) generally yields higher incremental-session accuracy, and the magnitude of the effect varies by dataset (the performance variance with respect to $c$ is smaller on CIFAR-100 than on miniImageNet).

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 5 claims performance increases monotonically with capacity c and depends on dataset. H2 provides a comprehensive capacity sweep that strongly supports the dataset-dependence part and the overall trend. However, P4 directly contradicts the monotonicity claim on miniImageNet (Table 11), showing clear non-monotonic behavior with a peak at c=80% followed by declines. The interaction between P4 and H2 means the sweep provides the data that disproves the monotonicity claim while supporting the dataset-dependence claim. The prior is moderate because the monotonicity part is false, but the trade-off characterization remains largely valid when corrected to non-monotonic. The conclusion must be revised.

nodes.title: Capacity and softness trade-offs in SoftNet

nodes.content: For ResNet18 on miniImageNet with $c=97\%$, fine-tuning minor weights at the Conv5x layer yields the best incremental performance. Additionally, optimal sparsity and accuracy vary by backbone: ResNet18 tends to prefer denser selected capacities while ResNet20 admits sparser solutions.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 6 claims ablation studies identify best fine-tuning layers and architecture-dependent sparsity. H3 provides a broad multi-architecture and multi-layer ablation that strongly supports the coarse findings: fine-tuning only a single conv layer is much better than fine-tuning all layers, and optimal capacity varies with architecture. However, P5 shows that the fine-grained layer ranking among conv layers (Table 3) is likely within noise, so the specific claim about Conv5x being best is unsupported. The prior is moderately high for the coarse claims but lower for the fine-grained layer claim. Overall credibility is moderate-high with a caution on over-specificity.

nodes.title: Layer-wise and architecture-wise ablation results

nodes.content: On a three-layer fully connected network (fc-4-25-30-3) trained on the Iris flower dataset (3-way classification, 150 samples) for 100 epochs, both HardNet (binary subnetwork) and SoftNet (soft subnetwork) yield flatter loss landscapes than a dense network; the SoftNet minor-subnetwork component helps find a flatter global minimum despite random scaling. On miniImageNet with capacity $c=30\%$ at Session 2, t-SNE visualizations indicate that SoftNet produces more discriminative and smoother class embeddings (better cluster separation for base and novel classes) than HardNet.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 7 claims that soft masks produce flatter loss landscapes and smoother embeddings. H1 provides a direct loss landscape measurement, but only on a toy model far from the operational ResNet/image setting (P6). The t-SNE evidence is qualitative and single-configuration (P7). The theoretical inequalities (C8) are also flawed (P8-P10). The interaction: H1 shows the claim is plausible in a toy setting, but P6 and P7 show that evidence for the operational setting is lacking. The credibility is low: the claim may be true but is not adequately demonstrated for the actual FSCIL models.

nodes.title: Soft masks produce flatter loss landscapes and smoother embeddings than dense or hard-masked networks

nodes.title: Optimization inequalities and convergence-rate statement for subnetworks

nodes.content:
On the miniImageNet TOPIC split, SoftNet at its best capacity (c=87%) achieves session-9 accuracy 54.68%, while the concurrent method ALICE (Peng et al., 2022) achieves 55.70%, both using the same ResNet18 backbone and 5-way 5-shot protocol. This direct comparison shows that SoftNet does not achieve the highest final accuracy on this benchmark.
      Table 6
      Peng, C., Zhao, K., Wang, T., Li, M., & Lovell, B. C. (2022). Few-shot class-incremental learning from an open-set perspective. In European Conference on Computer Vision.

metadata.failure_mode: If this premise is true (ALICE outperforms SoftNet on this benchmark), then the conclusion that SoftNet yields state-of-the-art FSCIL accuracy is false for the miniImageNet TOPIC split, which is a standard benchmark. Since the conclusion is stated globally without setting-specific caveats, the failure of one major benchmark refutes the unqualified claim.

refs.text: Peng, C., Zhao, K., Wang, T., Li, M., & Lovell, B. C. (2022). Few-shot class-incremental learning from an open-set perspective. In European Conference on Computer Vision.

metadata.weakness_reason: The paper's claim of "state-of-the-art performance" (abstract and conclusion) is contradicted by its own reported Table 6, where ALICE obtains higher session-9 accuracy. The paper acknowledges ALICE but still proclaims global state-of-the-art without qualification. The gap is small (1pp), but the paper does not run statistical tests; simply showing comparable numbers is not sufficient for a state-of-the-art claim. ALICE is a concurrent published method evaluated under the same conditions, so the comparison is fair. Overstating claims while including direct counter-evidence weakens the credibility of the conclusion.

nodes.title: ALICE outperforms SoftNet on miniImageNet TOPIC split

nodes.content:
Classification accuracy on CIFAR-100 and miniImageNet for few-shot class incremental learning (FSCIL) is reported as the mean over ten runs, but no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or error bars are provided for any of the entries.
      Tables 1, 2, 5, 6, 7

metadata.failure_mode: If the variance of the accuracy estimates is unknown, any claim of "higher" or "state-of-the-art" accuracy based solely on point estimates is scientifically incomplete. The conclusion that SoftNet yields higher accuracy could be false if the observed gaps are within the standard error. The strength of the conclusion is reduced from a quantitative ranking to a qualitative indication lacking statistical reliability.
metadata.weakness_reason: In few-shot settings, run-to-run variance is substantial due to random class splits, initialization, and data sampling. Standard FSCIL papers (e.g., F2M, Shi et al., 2021) report standard deviations. The absence of uncertainty quantification prevents the reader from assessing whether the reported improvements (e.g., +1.35pp on CIFAR-100 standard split) are statistically significant or within the noise range. Without this, the point estimates alone cannot support a strong claim of superiority.

nodes.title: No standard deviations reported for accuracy means

nodes.content:
In the experiments on CIFAR-100 and miniImageNet standard splits, the capacity parameter c is chosen per dataset via validation accuracy: CIFAR-100 standard split uses c=99%, and miniImageNet standard split uses c=80%. A fixed c was not used across all settings and no principled selection rule is provided; the choice is based on empirical tuning on each dataset.
      Tables 1, 2

metadata.failure_mode: If the premise is true (c selected per dataset post-hoc), the reported SOTA accuracy numbers are likely overestimates. The conclusion that SoftNet achieves higher accuracy than baselines is inflated relative to a fair comparison where all methods use the same hyperparameter selection protocol. The conclusion's validity is weaker than claimed; the true advantage of SoftNet may be smaller.
metadata.weakness_reason: When the best c is selected from a sweep per dataset, the reported accuracy is an optimistic estimate of the method's expected performance on a new dataset. This is a form of adaptive data-dependent hyperparameter selection that inflates apparent performance compared to a method using a fixed protocol. The paper acknowledges dataset dependence in Conclusion 5, but the SOTA claim in Conclusion 4 does not discount for this selection effect. Baselines may have been tuned differently or to a lesser extent, giving SoftNet an unfair advantage.

nodes.title: Capacity c selected per dataset post-hoc

nodes.content:
On the miniImageNet standard split, SoftNet session-9 accuracy at various c values is: c=50%: 47.60, c=60%: 48.57, c=70%: 49.69, c=80%: 50.48, c=90%: 50.39, c=93%: 48.45, c=95%: 49.84, c=97%: 50.24, c=99%: 50.04. The accuracy peaks at c=80% and then exhibits fluctuations with a decline at 90% and 93% before partial recovery, showing non-monotonic behavior.
      Table 11

metadata.failure_mode: If the premise is true (non-monotonic pattern), the conclusion's claim of monotonic improvement is false. The practical guidance derived from the conclusion (e.g., higher c always better) would be incorrect; instead, practitioners would need to tune c to find the optimum. The conclusion should be revised to state a more nuanced relationship.
metadata.weakness_reason: Conclusion 5 claims "overall accuracy monotonically improves with the selected major-subnetwork proportion c." The paper's own data directly contradicts this claim: accuracy at c=90% (50.39) is lower than at c=80% (50.48), c=93% (48.45) is lower, and the overall pattern is not monotonic. The wording "monotonically" is factually inaccurate based on the reported numbers. The correct description is that performance generally increases with c up to a point and then may plateau or vary.

nodes.title: Accuracy not monotonically increasing with c on miniImageNet

nodes.content:
In the layer-wise ablation on miniImageNet with c=97%, the session-9 accuracy for Conv2x is 50.19, Conv3x 50.15, Conv4x 50.17, Conv5x 50.24, and All 25.64. The difference between the best conv layer (Conv5x) and the worst (Conv3x) is 0.09 percentage points. No standard deviations are reported for these numbers.
      Table 3

metadata.failure_mode: If this premise is true (differences are noise), the conclusion's specific layer recommendation (Conv5x) is unsupported. The robust finding is that fine-tuning any single conv layer works similarly well, while fine-tuning all layers is harmful. The paper's layer-wise conclusion would need to be revised to reflect this coarser insight.
metadata.weakness_reason: The differences among conv layers (max 0.09pp) are far smaller than typical standard errors in 5-way 5-shot FSCIL experiments (often 0.5-1.0pp, as seen in F2M, Shi et al., 2021). Without any uncertainty quantification, the observed ordering is likely a result of random variation rather than a true layer-specific effect. The conclusion that "the best performances involve fine-tuning at the Conv5x layer" overstates what the data can support.

nodes.title: Layer-wise differences in Table 3 are within noise level

nodes.content:
The loss landscape visualization supporting the claim that subnetworks (HardNet and SoftNet) yield flatter minima than dense networks is conducted on a three-layer fully-connected network with architecture fc-4-25-30-3, trained on the Iris flower dataset (3-way classification, 150 samples) for 100 epochs. This is not the ResNet backbone or image dataset used in the FSCIL experiments.
      Figure 7

metadata.failure_mode: If the premise is true (the toy experiment does not transfer to ResNets), then the primary empirical support for Claim 7's flatness statement is absent for the models actually used. The conclusion that soft masks produce flatter loss landscapes in FSCIL becomes unsupported, leaving only the weak t-SNE evidence (P7) and the flawed theoretical analysis (P8-P10). The conclusion's credibility is severely undermined.
metadata.weakness_reason: The loss landscape properties of deep ResNets on high-dimensional image data (CIFAR-100: 60 classes, 32x32 images) are known to differ substantially from those of tiny fully-connected networks on low-dimensional toy data. The paper provides no argument or evidence that the flatness observed in the toy model transfers to the operational architecture. The conclusion about flatness in the ResNet-based FSCIL setting therefore lacks empirical justification from this experiment.

nodes.title: Loss landscape analysis uses a toy model, not the operational FSCIL setup

nodes.content:
The t-SNE embedding comparison between HardNet and SoftNet is shown for only one configuration: capacity c=30% at Session 2 on miniImageNet. The evaluation is visual and qualitative; no quantitative metrics such as silhouette score, intra/inter-class distance ratio, or nearest-class-mean accuracy on the embedding space are provided.
      Figure 6

metadata.failure_mode: If the t-SNE evidence is unreliable or insufficient, the claim about embedding quality lacks quantitative support. Combined with P6, Conclusion 7 is left with no credible empirical evidence in the actual experimental setting. The conclusion that soft masks improve embedding structure would be reduced to speculation.
metadata.weakness_reason: t-SNE visualizations are sensitive to hyperparameters and can produce misleading impressions of separation. A single snapshot at one capacity and one session does not demonstrate consistent superiority of SoftNet embeddings. Without quantitative comparisons, the claim that SoftNet produces "more discriminative and smoother class embeddings" is based on subjective interpretation of two plots. The visual difference in Figure 6 is subtle and not rigorously quantified.

nodes.title: t-SNE visualization is qualitative and single-configuration

nodes.content:
The theoretical derivation of masked-gradient inequalities assumes the objective function $R: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuously differentiable with Lipschitz continuous gradient (constant $L>0$). The neural networks used throughout the experiments (ResNets with ReLU activations) are piecewise linear and not continuously differentiable; the gradient is not Lipschitz continuous over the parameter space due to discontinuities at the switching points of the ReLU function.
      Eq. (6), Eq. (7), Eq. (8), Eq. (9)

metadata.failure_mode: If the Lipschitz assumption fails, Eqs. (7)-(9) are not valid for the paper's models. The conclusion that subnetworks obey better worst-case rate bounds and that soft masks have lower normalized gradient Lipschitz ratios is theoretically unsupported. The entire theoretical framework in Appendix C is called into question. Conclusion 8 loses its formal justification.
metadata.weakness_reason: The Lipschitz gradient condition is violated by any network with ReLU activations because the gradient jumps at the hyperplane where a neuron switches between active and inactive states. The paper uses ResNets with ReLU in all experiments, yet the derived inequalities rely on this assumption. The paper does not discuss this violation or argue that the results hold in a weaker sense (e.g., almost everywhere). The inequalities are therefore not mathematically valid statements for the models under study.

nodes.title: Lipschitz gradient assumption does not hold for ReLU networks

nodes.content:
The derivation of the inequality comparing normalized gradient Lipschitz ratios for hard and soft masks requires that $R(\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{hard}) \approx R(\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{soft})$ (the loss values under the two masks are close). The paper states this condition but provides no empirical verification that the losses are indeed close for any of the actual training runs in the experiments.
      Eq. (9)

metadata.failure_mode: If the equality condition is violated, inequality (9) cannot be asserted. The conclusion that soft masks produce flatter dynamics than hard masks via this Lipschitz ratio argument is unsupported. Conclusion 8's comparative claim between hard and soft masks is left unsubstantiated.
metadata.weakness_reason: The condition is critical: if the losses are not close, the inequality (9) does not follow from the premises. The paper could easily have computed and reported the actual loss values for hard and soft masks at the end of base training. The absence of this check leaves the derivation as an assumption rather than a demonstrated result. In practice, the random scaling of minor parameters by uniform U(0,1) introduces variation that may cause losses to differ meaningfully.

nodes.title: Equality R(theta*m_hard)≈R(theta*m_soft) is unverified

nodes.content:
The worst-case convergence rate $R(\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}) = \mathcal{O}(1/\|\boldsymbol{m}\|_1^2)$ for subnetworks is cited from Ye et al. (2020), who derive this bound for greedy forward selection in convex optimization settings. The rate is applied to non-convex neural network training without justification that the bound remains valid.
      Ye, M., Gong, C., Nie, L., Zhou, D., Klivans, A., & Liu, Q. (2020). Good subnetworks provably exist: Pruning via greedy forward selection. In International Conference on Machine Learning.

metadata.failure_mode: If the bound does not apply to non-convex NN training, the claim that subnetworks achieve a faster worst-case rate than dense networks is unsupported by the cited reference. Combined with P8 and P9, Conclusion 8's entire theoretical apparatus is compromised, leaving no valid formal support for the superiority of subnetworks in terms of convergence.

refs.text: Ye, M., Gong, C., Nie, L., Zhou, D., Klivans, A., & Liu, Q. (2020). Good subnetworks provably exist: Pruning via greedy forward selection. In International Conference on Machine Learning.

metadata.weakness_reason: Convergence bounds for convex problems generally do not transfer to non-convex neural network training, where the optimization landscape has many local minima and saddle points. The paper does not argue that the bound holds for non-convex objectives or that the specific training procedure (SGD with metric-based loss) satisfies the required conditions. The cited reference is used out of its established regime.

nodes.title: Convergence rate bound from Ye et al. applies to convex objectives only

nodes.content: The Regularized Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (RLTH) states that a randomly-initialized dense neural network contains a regularized subnetwork capable of retaining prior class knowledge and learning new classes through isolated training. No direct evidence is provided that such a subnetwork exists prior to training; the only demonstration is that SoftNet, which jointly trains soft masks alongside model weights, achieves good FSCIL performance. This demonstrates that a soft-masked network can be trained, not that it exists inherently in a random initialization.

metadata.failure_mode: If RLTH is not validated, the paper's foundational conceptual contribution is unsupported. The specific claim that a randomly-initialized network inherently contains a regularized subnetwork with these properties is neither proven nor demonstrated. The paper's novelty reduces to the algorithm design rather than the verification of a hypothesis. The conclusion would need to be retracted or reformulated as a conjecture.
metadata.weakness_reason: The original Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (Frankle & Carbin, 2019) was validated by finding winning tickets through pruning and retraining that preserved the original initialization. RLTH is stated as a hypothesis, but the paper does not attempt to verify it: it does not isolate a subnetwork from a random initialization and show it can incrementally learn; instead, it jointly trains masks and weights, which is a different operation. The conclusion as presented states RLTH as a finding of the paper, but the work does not provide the necessary evidence (e.g., a pruning-at-initialization experiment) to substantiate it.

nodes.title: RLTH is not empirically validated

nodes.content: The paper provides empirical loss landscape visualizations (Figure 7) comparing DenseNet, HardNet, and SoftNet on a three-layer fully-connected network (fc-4-25-30-3) trained on the Iris flower dataset (3-way classification, 150 samples, 100 epochs) using Hessian eigenvector analysis (Yao et al., 2020) to produce 2D loss contours. The visualization shows that subnetworks (both HardNet and SoftNet) produce flatter loss contours than the dense network, and SoftNet's minor subnetwork helps find a flat global minimum despite random scaling.

metadata.credit: The visualization provides direct empirical evidence that, in a controlled toy setting, joint training with the soft-mask procedure yields a flatter minimum than dense training. This preempts the failure mode where the flatness claim would have zero empirical support (relying only on speculation or flawed theory). It underwrites the qualitative direction of the conclusion—soft masks do not harm landscape flatness—within a limited, bounded regime. The scope of credit is regime-bounded: the experiment uses a tiny network and dataset, but it is a clean demonstration of the effect. Without this figure, the paper's claim about flatness would have no direct visual evidence at all.

nodes.title: Loss landscape visualization on toy model

nodes.content: For both HardNet and SoftNet on CIFAR-100 (Table 9) and miniImageNet (Table 11), the paper reports session-by-session accuracy for capacity c from 10% to 99% in steps of 10% or finer (including 93%, 95%, 97%, 99%), and Figure 2 visualizes overall, base, and novel class performances as functions of c for both datasets.

metadata.credit: The comprehensive capacity sweep preempts the failure mode where claims about the effect of capacity would be based on a single c value or a narrow range, which would be insufficient to characterize the dependence. It provides a full empirical mapping of accuracy as a function of c, supporting the conclusion that performance varies with c and depends on dataset. Without these tables and figures, the conclusion's claim about dataset-dependent trade-offs would be unsupported. The scope of credit: it quantitatively characterizes the relationship for the two datasets used, allowing practitioners to see the shape of the curve and the optimal ranges.

nodes.title: Comprehensive capacity sweeps across c values

nodes.content: The paper presents layer-wise fine-tuning experiments on miniImageNet with ResNet18 (c=97%) in Table 3, showing accuracy for fine-tuning Conv2x through Conv5x and All layers. It also presents architecture-wise comparisons on CIFAR-100 for ResNet18, ResNet20, ResNet32, and ResNet50 at multiple c values in Table 4. This covers multiple backbones, multiple layers, and multiple capacities in a systematic ablation.

metadata.credit: The ablations preempt the failure mode where guidelines for layer selection and architecture choice would be based on a single architecture or no ablation at all. They provide strong evidence that fine-tuning only a single conv layer (versus all layers) is critical (Table 3: All-layer fine-tuning yields 25.64 vs conv layers ~50.2 in session-9), and that optimal capacity varies with architecture (Table 4). These are practically important and robust findings that are well-supported by the data. The scope of credit: the coarse findings (single-layer fine-tuning is essential; capacity choice is architecture-dependent) are fully underwritten. The fine-grained layer ranking among conv layers is not robust (P5), but the coarse findings remain valuable.

nodes.title: Multi-architecture and layer-wise ablations

steps.reasoning:
State the few-shot class-incremental learning (FSCIL) problem setting and its two principal challenges: catastrophic forgetting and overfitting. Define the FSCIL training sequence as a sequence of $T$ sessions $\{\mathcal{D}^{1},\ldots,\mathcal{D}^{T}\}$ where session $t$ has training examples $\mathcal{D}^{t}=\{z_i^t=(\boldsymbol{x}_i^t,y_i^t)\}_{i=1}^{n_t}$ and the model is a parametric predictor $f(\cdot;\boldsymbol{\theta})$ with parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^d$. Note that in FSCIL the base session ($t=1$) typically has many examples per class whereas subsequent sessions ($t\ge2$) are $N$-way $K$-shot tasks with very few examples per class, causing (a) catastrophic forgetting (loss of prior-task performance when updating $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ on new sessions) and (b) overfitting when updating $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ on few new examples.
[Goodfellow et al., 2013]

Recall the original Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) definition used as motivation: LTH posits that, within a randomly-initialized overparameterized dense neural network with parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}$, there exist sparse binary subnetworks (binary masks $\boldsymbol{m}\in\{0,1\}^{|\boldsymbol{\theta}|}$) whose masked parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}$ can be trained to match or exceed dense-network performance. Declare that this prior motivates searching for subnetworks that preserve prior knowledge while enabling adaptation.
[Frankle and Carbin, 2019]

Introduce the need to generalize the binary (hard) subnetwork concept to a smooth (non-binary) one to address FSCIL-specific trade-offs: define a soft mask $\boldsymbol{m}\in[0,1]^{|\boldsymbol{\theta}|}$ (component-wise in the interval $[0,1]$) so that the masked parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}$ act as a regularized parameter subspace that (i) can be largely preserved to retain base-session class knowledge, and (ii) contains continuously-valued degrees of freedom for isolated fine-tuning to learn new classes without catastrophically altering preserved components.

Formalize the Regularized Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (RLTH) as the statement that a randomly-initialized dense neural network contains a regularized subnetwork (expressed by a smooth mask $\boldsymbol{m}\in[0,1]^{|\boldsymbol{\theta}|}$) that can both retain prior class knowledge and provide room to learn new class knowledge through isolated training of the subnetwork; emphasize that RLTH generalizes the binary winning-ticket view by allowing continuous (soft) mask values in $[0,1]$ so the subnetwork can act as a regularized parameter subspace for incremental few-shot adaptation.

Support RLTH by connecting it to the optimization objective for a masked model: define a session-$t$ masked optimization objective over mask $\boldsymbol{m}_t\in[0,1]^{|\boldsymbol{\theta}|}$ as minimizing the empirical session loss
$$
\frac{1}{n_t}\sum_{i=1}^{n_t}\mathcal{L}_t\!\big(f(\boldsymbol{x}_i^t;\,\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_t),\,y_i^t\big)
$$
subject to a sparsity/selected-capacity constraint $|\boldsymbol{m}_t|\le c$ (where $|\cdot|$ denotes number or proportion of selected parameters and $c\ll|\boldsymbol{\theta}|$ denotes the selected proportion). Observe that allowing $\boldsymbol{m}_t\in[0,1]^{|\boldsymbol{\theta}|}$ makes the subnetwork both a selection mask and a continuous regularizer on parameter magnitudes, consistent with the RLTH formulation.

Note the operational decomposition of a soft mask used to realize RLTH in the paper: express $\boldsymbol{m}_{soft}$ as the element-wise sum $\boldsymbol{m}_{soft}=\boldsymbol{m}_{major}\oplus\boldsymbol{m}_{minor}$ where $\boldsymbol{m}_{major}$ is a (layer-wise) binary indicator selecting a top-$c\%$ of weights and $\boldsymbol{m}_{minor}$ provides continuous-valued residuals in $[0,1]$ (sampled from $U(0,1)$ in the authors' instantiation) on the remaining parameters. Explain that this two-part decomposition operationalizes RLTH by designating the major component for knowledge retention and the minor component for controlled adaptation.

Start from the Regularized Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (RLTH) (established): the method should produce a smooth (non-binary) subnetwork mask $\boldsymbol{m}_{soft}\in[0,1]^{|\boldsymbol{\theta}|}$ that partitions parameters into a preserved major component and an adaptable minor component to address catastrophic forgetting and overfitting in FSCIL.

Associate each learnable model weight with a learnable weight score vector $\boldsymbol{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\boldsymbol{\theta}|}$ that numerically indicates per-weight importance; define the layer-wise top-$c\%$ indicator operator $\mathbb{1}_{\text{top-}c\%}(\boldsymbol{s})$ which produces a binary mask valued $1$ for the top-$c\%$ entries of $\boldsymbol{s}$ (per layer) and $0$ otherwise. Use these definitions to define the major binary mask
$$
\boldsymbol{m}_{major}=\mathbb{1}_{\text{top-}c\%}(\boldsymbol{s}).
$$

Define the minor (continuous) mask $\boldsymbol{m}_{minor}$ as a continuous-valued mask on the remaining parameters: in the authors' operational scheme, sample $\boldsymbol{m}_{minor}$ entries from the uniform distribution on $(0,1)$ for indices not selected by the major mask, i.e., $\boldsymbol{m}_{minor}\sim U(0,1)$ on the complement of the top-$c\%$ indices and $0$ (or appropriately small) on top-$c\%$ indices. Then define the overall soft mask $\boldsymbol{m}_{soft}$ as the elementwise sum
$$
\boldsymbol{m}_{soft}=\boldsymbol{m}_{major}\oplus\boldsymbol{m}_{minor},
$$
so that $\boldsymbol{m}_{soft}\in[0,1]^{|\boldsymbol{\theta}|}$ with $\boldsymbol{m}_{major}$ providing binary ’locked’ components and $\boldsymbol{m}_{minor}$ providing soft, tunable components.
Fig. 1

Describe the joint optimization during the base session ($t=1$): initialize model weights $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ and score weights $\boldsymbol{s}$ randomly; for each mini-batch compute the base-session loss using the masked model $f(\cdot;\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{soft})$ and update both model weights and scores. The model-weight update is performed by applying element-wise masking to the gradient: with base-session learning rate $\alpha$, update
$$
\boldsymbol{\theta}\leftarrow\boldsymbol{\theta}-\alpha\Big(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\theta}}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{soft}\Big),
$$
where $\odot$ denotes element-wise product.

Explain the score updates and the straight-through estimator (STE) technicality: since $\boldsymbol{m}_{major}$ is obtained via an indicator function on $\boldsymbol{s}$ and the indicator has zero derivative almost everywhere, directly backpropagating through $\mathbb{1}_{\text{top-}c\%}(\boldsymbol{s})$ is infeasible. Therefore apply the Straight-through Estimator (STE) for $\boldsymbol{s}$: compute the surrogate gradient and update the scores with the same element-wise masking:
$$
\boldsymbol{s}\leftarrow\boldsymbol{s}-\alpha\Big(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\boldsymbol{s}}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{soft}\Big),
$$
treating the indicator as identity in the backward pass. Cite the STE literature invoked by the authors for justification.
[Hinton, 2012]
[Bengio et al., 2013]

Summarize the base-session inner loop operationally as implemented in the paper's algorithm: at each epoch obtain $\boldsymbol{m}_{soft}$ from the current $\boldsymbol{s}$ (top-$c\%$ for $\boldsymbol{m}_{major}$ and sampled continuous values for $\boldsymbol{m}_{minor}$), compute batch loss $\mathcal{L}_{base}(\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{soft};\boldsymbol{b})$, update $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ by masked gradient descent, and update $\boldsymbol{s}$ using STE-masked gradient descent. Refer to the algorithm pseudocode named Algorithm 1 in the paper that summarizes this procedure.
Algorithm 1

Describe the incremental-session ($t\ge2$) operational rule derived from the soft-mask decomposition: during incremental few-shot sessions freeze the major subnetwork parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{major}$ (to preserve base-session class knowledge) and fine-tune only the minor parameters corresponding to $\boldsymbol{m}_{minor}$. Concretely, with incremental learning rate $\beta$, update the model parameters with element-wise masking by $\boldsymbol{m}_{minor}$:
$$
\boldsymbol{\theta}\leftarrow\boldsymbol{\theta}-\beta\Big(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\theta}}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{minor}\Big).
$$
State that scores $\boldsymbol{s}$ and $\boldsymbol{m}_{soft}$ are kept from the base session and not updated during incremental fine-tuning in the authors' procedure.
Algorithm 1

Collectively label this operational masking-based FSCIL method as Soft-SubNetworks (SoftNet): the method (a) obtains a soft mask $\boldsymbol{m}_{soft}$ via score-based top-$c\%$ selection plus continuous minor-mask sampling during base training, (b) jointly updates $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ and $\boldsymbol{s}$ during base training using STE and masked gradients as specified above, and (c) for incremental sessions freezes the major subnetwork and fine-tunes only the minor subnetwork parameters. Note that the paper presents this full flow as Algorithm 1 and illustrates it schematically (schematic depiction of major/minor subnetworks and incremental updates).
Fig. 1
Algorithm 1

Take the SoftNet algorithm and its operational masking scheme as established starting points: the soft mask $\boldsymbol{m}_{soft}=\boldsymbol{m}_{major}\oplus\boldsymbol{m}_{minor}$ is obtained at base training and in incremental sessions the model parameters used are $\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{soft}$ while only minor parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{minor}$ are updated.

Specify the metric-based fine-tuning loss used during incremental sessions: define the per-example metric loss using cosine distance $d(\cdot,\cdot)$ and class prototypes $\boldsymbol{p}_o$ for classes $o$ in the set of encountered classes $\mathcal{O}=\bigcup_{i=1}^t\mathcal{O}^i$. For a dataset $\mathcal{D}$ (the union of current-session data and stored exemplars) the metric loss is:
$$
\mathcal{L}_{m}(z;\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{soft})=-\sum_{z\in\mathcal{D}}\sum_{o\in\mathcal{O}}\mathbb{1}(y=o)\log\frac{e^{-d\!\left(\boldsymbol{p}_o,\;f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{soft})\right)}}{\sum_{o_k\in\mathcal{O}}e^{-d\!\left(\boldsymbol{p}_{o_k},\;f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{soft})\right)}},
$$
where $\mathbb{1}(\cdot)$ is the indicator function and $f(\cdot;\cdot)$ denotes the feature extractor.
Eq. (5)

Define class prototypes used in the metric loss: for a class $o$ with $N_o$ training examples, define the prototype vector $\boldsymbol{p}_o$ as the mean embedding of class-$o$ examples under the masked feature extractor:
$$
\boldsymbol{p}_o=\frac{1}{N_o}\sum_i \mathbb{1}(y_i=o)\,f(\boldsymbol{x}_i;\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{soft}).
$$
State that prototypes for base classes are computed and stored in the base session; prototypes for new classes are computed during incremental sessions and also saved for evaluation.

Explain the cosine distance choice rationale invoked by the authors: the authors argue that cosine distance $d(\cdot,\cdot)$ yields a normalized informative measurement that better reflects directional similarity between representations than Euclidean distance in some cases (Euclidean distance can place points at equal Euclidean distance from a prototype while failing to reflect directional alignment). Therefore SoftNet fine-tunes minor weights using the cosine-based metric loss above to mitigate the few-shot overfitting and provide stable prototype estimates.
[Shi et al., 2021]

Describe the inference-time classifier used by SoftNet after incremental fine-tuning: define the nearest-class-mean (NCM) classifier where, given a test input $\boldsymbol{x}$, the embedding $f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{soft})$ is computed and the predicted class is the prototype index minimizing Euclidean distance $d_u(\cdot,\cdot)$ in feature space:
$$
o^*=\arg\min_{o\in\mathcal{O}} d_u\!\big(f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{soft}),\;\boldsymbol{p}_o\big).
$$
Cite the nearest-class-mean (NCM) procedure as the inference mechanism used by the authors.
[Mensink et al., 2013]
Take SoftNet's algorithmic specification (soft masks, base-session joint optimization, incremental minor-weight fine-tuning) as established starting material.

Describe the experimental protocol used to evaluate SoftNet on standard FSCIL benchmarks: datasets include CIFAR-100 and miniImageNet; the experimental split uses 60 base classes and 40 novel classes with eight novel sessions each forming 5-way 5-shot problems; backbone network is ResNet18; each algorithm is run ten times per split and mean accuracy is reported. State that results are presented per session and compared to strong baselines including cRT (classifier re-training), HardNet, FSLL, iCaRL, Rebalance, TOPIC, and F2M.

Report the CIFAR-100 ResNet18 results cited in the paper as direct evidence: for SoftNet with selected proportion $c=99\%$ (ResNet18 backbone) the reported session-1 (base-session) accuracy is $72.62\%$ and the session-9 (final incremental session) accuracy is $46.63\%$. State that these numbers are taken from the experimental results table comparing to baselines and that the authors report a relative gap of $+1.35$ percentage points versus the cRT reference in the CIFAR-100 table.
Table 1
[Shi et al., 2021]

Report the miniImageNet ResNet18 results cited in the paper as direct evidence: for SoftNet with selected proportion $c=80\%$ (ResNet18 backbone) the reported session-1 accuracy is $76.63\%$ and the session-9 accuracy is $50.48\%$. State that the authors report a relative gap of $+5.63$ percentage points versus the cRT reference in the miniImageNet table.
Table 2

Note the authors' broader empirical claim: similar superior or competitive numbers are reported across additional splits and datasets (e.g., TOPIC splits and CUB-200-2011). Reference the TOPIC-split and CUB experimental tables where SoftNet's numbers are compared against recent state-of-the-art methods and cRT, showing SoftNet either attains state-of-the-art or is competitive depending on dataset and capacity choice.
Table 5
Table 7

Conclude that the empirical evidence presented (the session-wise accuracy values, gaps relative to cRT, and comparisons across multiple baselines and datasets) establishes that SoftNet attains higher incremental accuracy than the cited strong baselines on standard FSCIL benchmarks under the reported experimental conditions.
Treat the SoftNet method and its experimental protocol as known starting points.

Report the authors' empirical observation relating selected-capacity proportion $c$ to performance: summarize the stated experimental finding that as the proportion $c$ of parameters selected into the major subnetwork increases, SoftNet's overall incremental accuracy monotonically improves in the reported experiments (i.e., larger $c$ → higher overall session accuracy in the presented curves and tables).
Figure 2

Make explicit the dataset dependence observation the authors provide: the paper states that the magnitude of the performance change with respect to $c$ varies by dataset, specifically noting that performance variance across different $c$ values is smaller on CIFAR-100 than on miniImageNet (i.e., miniImageNet shows larger sensitivity to $c$ choices), and that the best-performing $c$ can differ by dataset and architecture.
Figure 2

Point to the presentation of per-capacity accuracy data that supports these claims: the authors provide per-capacity tables (e.g., full capacity tables in Appendix, Table 9 for CIFAR-100 and Table 11 for miniImageNet) and per-capacity curves (Figure 2) which demonstrate the monotonic trend and dataset-dependent variance described above.
Table 9
Table 11

Conclude that the empirical evidence in the paper establishes the claimed capacity/softness trade-offs: SoftNet's overall accuracy increases with the selected major-subnetwork proportion $c$ in the reported experiments, and the sensitivity of performance to $c$ depends on dataset (smaller variance on CIFAR-100 than on miniImageNet), as shown by the per-capacity curves and full capacity tables.
Take SoftNet (its soft masks and incremental fine-tuning of minor parameters) and the experimental setup as established starting points.

Describe the layer-wise ablation experimental design the authors use: with a fixed selected proportion $c$ (the authors report $c=97\%$ in the cited ablation), they freeze all minor weights except those in a single specified layer-block (e.g., Conv2x, Conv3x, Conv4x, Conv5x in ResNet18 notation), and fine-tune only that layer's minor weights during incremental sessions, reporting session-wise accuracies for each choice.

Report the specific layer-wise empirical result the authors present for ResNet18 on miniImageNet with $c=97\%$: Table 3 lists per-session accuracies for the layer-wise experiments and shows that fine-tuning the minor weights at the Conv5x layer yields the best incremental performance (Conv5x row in the table attains the highest session-9 accuracy among the Conv2x–Conv5x and 'All' scenarios), while the 'All' scenario (fine-tuning all minor weights across all layers) performs poorly (large forgetting/overfitting).
Table 3

Explain the interpretation the authors provide: features computed by lower layers are more general and reusable across classes, whereas higher-layer features are more class-specific and therefore updating higher-layer minor weights (e.g., Conv5x) is most beneficial for learning novel classes in FSCIL while preserving general lower-layer representations, which is consistent with the observed best performance for Conv5x fine-tuning.

Describe the architecture-wise ablation design and findings: the authors evaluate SoftNet across multiple backbone architectures (ResNet18, ResNet20, ResNet32, ResNet50) and varying $c$ values, reporting results in an architecture-wise table. They observe that optimal sparsity and accuracy vary by backbone: e.g., ResNet18 tends to perform best when using denser selected capacities (the paper reports ResNet18 best at $c=99\%$ in the CIFAR-100 experiments), whereas ResNet20 attains optimal performance at a sparser selected capacity (the paper reports ResNet20 optimum around $c=90\%$).
Table 4

Conclude that the ablation studies identify both the best fine-tuning layers (Conv5x for ResNet18 in the reported miniImageNet $c=97\%$ experiments) and that optimal sparsity and accuracy are architecture-dependent (ResNet18 favoring denser $c$ while ResNet20 preferring sparser $c$), supporting the stated conclusion that layer-wise and architecture-wise ablations identify best fine-tuning layers and architecture-dependent sparsity.

Take as given: (a) the SoftNet method specification (soft masks, major/minor decomposition, minor-only incremental fine-tuning) and (b) the optimization inequalities and masked-gradient reasoning previously established (the smaller normalized Lipschitz ratio for denser soft masks under certain approximations), which together provide theoretical motivation that subnetworks—especially soft masks with larger $\|\boldsymbol{m}\|_1$—can exhibit flatter effective loss landscapes.
[Ye et al., 2020]

Describe the empirical loss-landscape evidence the authors present: they compute loss-landscape visualizations using perturbations along two Hessian eigenvectors (i.e., visualize loss on a 2D plane spanned by two Hessian eigenvectors) for three trained models — a dense network, a hard-masked subnetwork (HardNet), and a soft-masked subnetwork (SoftNet). The plotted loss landscapes show that subnetworks (both HardNet and SoftNet) occupy flatter regions (i.e., smaller curvature, broader basins) compared to the dense network, and the SoftNet minor-subnetwork component helps find a flatter global minimum despite random scaling in training; the authors present these plots as empirical support for flatter minima of subnetworks.
Figure 7

State the t-SNE embedding evidence the authors provide: the authors produce two-dimensional t-SNE visualizations of learned embeddings comparing HardNet and SoftNet (e.g., both at $c=30\%$ in a session-2 embedding comparison). The reported observations are that SoftNet embeddings show better cluster separation and more discriminative structure for both base-class and novel-class points than HardNet in the presented examples, which the authors interpret as smoother and more discriminative representations produced by soft masks.
Figure 6

Bridge the theoretical and empirical evidence: invoke the optimization inequalities result (that masked/dense normalization of gradient Lipschitz ratios suggests subnetworks can have smaller normalized gradient changes, i.e., flatter effective loss surfaces) and state that the empirical loss-landscape visualizations corroborate this by showing subnetworks achieve visibly flatter minima than dense networks, and that SoftNet (with its minor soft component) attains an even flatter global minimum relative to HardNet in the authors' experiments.
Figure 7

Record the authors' heuristic/interpretative claim without further proof: the paper asserts (and supports empirically) that the soft minor-subnetwork acts as a regularizer producing smoother embeddings and flatter loss geometry, which the authors associate with better robustness to random perturbations and improved generalization/retention in FSCIL; note that part of this argument is heuristic and backed primarily by empirical visualization rather than formal proof in the paper.

State the foundational smoothness assumption used for the analysis: let $R:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ denote the objective (population or empirical loss) and assume $R$ is continuously differentiable with gradient $\nabla R:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d$ that is Lipschitz-continuous with Lipschitz constant $L>0$. Explicitly write the Lipschitz-gradient inequality:
$$
\|\nabla R(\boldsymbol{\theta})-\nabla R(\boldsymbol{\theta}')\|_2 \le L\|\boldsymbol{\theta}-\boldsymbol{\theta}'\|\quad\text{for all }\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\theta}'\in\mathbb{R}^d,
$$
where $\|\cdot\|_2$ denotes the Euclidean norm and $\|\cdot\|$ denotes the same Euclidean norm.
[Bottou et al., 2018]

Define the masked/ subnetwork gradient-smoothness inequality by applying the same Lipschitz assumption to masked parameters: for a binary mask $\boldsymbol{m}\in\{0,1\}^{|\boldsymbol{\theta}|}$ (or more generally for a mask in $[0,1]^{|\boldsymbol{\theta}|}$ interpreted elementwise), state the masked gradient Lipschitz inequality:
$$
\|\nabla R(\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m})-\nabla R(\boldsymbol{\theta}'\odot\boldsymbol{m})\|_2 \le L\|(\boldsymbol{\theta}-\boldsymbol{\theta}')\odot\boldsymbol{m}\|\quad\text{for all }\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\theta}'\in\mathbb{R}^d,
$$
where $\odot$ denotes element-wise product and norms are Euclidean.

Cite the theoretical rate bound for subnetworks from prior work the authors invoke: reference the result that, under appropriate conditions, subnetworks can achieve a faster worst-case convergence-rate bound of the form
$$
R(\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m})=\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{1}{\|\boldsymbol{m}\|_1^2}\right),
$$
where $\|\boldsymbol{m}\|_1$ denotes the $\ell_1$ norm of the mask (i.e., the sum of mask entries, equal to the number of selected parameters for binary masks). Attribute this rate to the cited prior theoretical work.
[Ye et al., 2020]

Derive a comparative inequality to connect masked gradients and flatness intuition: under the assumptions and using the prior theoretical relation, the authors present the inequality
$$
\frac{\|\nabla R(\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m})-\nabla R(\boldsymbol{\theta}'\odot\boldsymbol{m})\|_2}{\|(\boldsymbol{\theta}-\boldsymbol{\theta}')\odot\boldsymbol{m}\|} < \frac{\|\nabla R(\boldsymbol{\theta})-\nabla R(\boldsymbol{\theta}')\|_2}{\|\boldsymbol{\theta}-\boldsymbol{\theta}'\|} \le L,
$$
which indicates that the normalized change in masked gradients can be strictly smaller than that of the full parameter vector, suggesting a flatter effective loss landscape for the subnetwork. Note that the paper references the relationship $R(\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m})\ll R^*(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ and $\|(\boldsymbol{\theta}-\boldsymbol{\theta}')\odot\boldsymbol{m}\|<\|\boldsymbol{\theta}-\boldsymbol{\theta}'\|$ to motivate the inequality.

State the comparative inequality between hard (binary) and soft (continuous) masks the authors derive: assuming that $R(\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{hard})\approx R(\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{soft})$ (i.e., the objective values of the two masked solutions are approximately equal) and that $\|\boldsymbol{m}_{hard}\|_1<\|\boldsymbol{m}_{soft}\|_1$ (i.e., the hard mask selects fewer parameters in $\ell_1$ sense), then the authors deduce the inequality
$$
\frac{\|\nabla R(\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{hard})-\nabla R(\boldsymbol{\theta}'\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{hard})\|_2}{\|(\boldsymbol{\theta}-\boldsymbol{\theta}')\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{hard}\|} \ge
\frac{\|\nabla R(\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{soft})-\nabla R(\boldsymbol{\theta}'\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{soft})\|_2}{\|(\boldsymbol{\theta}-\boldsymbol{\theta}')\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{soft}\|},
$$
noting that equality holds only if $\|\boldsymbol{m}_{hard}\|_1=\|\boldsymbol{m}_{soft}\|_1$. Interpret this as the normalized gradient Lipschitz ratio being larger for the (sparser) hard mask than for the (denser) soft mask under the stated approximations.

Clarify assumptions and heuristic elements: record that the step asserting $R(\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{hard})\approx R(\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_{soft})$ is an approximate equality the authors invoke to compare normalized gradient magnitudes, and that the theoretical rate $R(\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m})=\mathcal{O}(1/\|\boldsymbol{m}\|_1^2)$ is cited from prior work rather than derived in full in the paper.
[Ye et al., 2020]

open_questions.content: The paper explicitly acknowledges and leaves several scientific and practical issues unresolved: (1) Stability of major-subnetwork protection: once the major subnetwork is selected/tuned, further adjustments to those parameters can still cause potential loss of previously acquired base-session knowledge; the mechanism to detect or adapt the model sparsity online so that new-session learners know how to preserve base knowledge remains open. (2) Privacy and robustness of the mask encoding: because SoftNet explicitly divides parameters by magnitude and exposes mask structure, the selected essential parameters may be vulnerable to intentional model attacks or information leakage; developing compact/compressed encodings or defenses for the binary/soft mask to reduce capacity and protect task knowledge is an unresolved engineering challenge. (3) Long-range scalability and capacity expansion for long sequences: the current SoftNet procedure freezes the major subnetwork and adapts minor parameters for a modest number of few-shot sessions; how to scale the approach (e.g., by expanding parameters or dynamically reallocating capacity) to much longer sequences of incoming classes (full CIL regimes) without revisiting data is left for future work. (4) Mask-selection criteria and deployment guidelines: while the paper provides empirical capacity ($c$) curves and architecture-dependent observations, principled rules to choose $c$ or to automatically adapt softness per layer/dataset for arbitrary architectures remain open. These limitations and future directions are explicitly stated by the authors.
